newsitem.title: USA: White House avoids comment on Paula Jones case.
newsitem.headline: White House avoids comment on Paula Jones case.

text.p: The White House avoided comment on the Supreme Court's hearing on Monday on whether the sexual harassment suit by Paula Jones should be allowed to proceed while President Bill Clinton is in office.

The nine justices will consider for the first time in hour-long arguments by opposing lawyers whether a sitting president may face civil legal action seeking damages for events that took place before he took office.

The high court will focus on when Jones's lawsuit may go forward, not the merits of her allegations that Clinton made unwanted sexual advances in 1991 in a Little Rock hotel room when he was governor of Arkansas and she was a state employee.
A ruling is due by the end of the court's term in June.

White House spokesman Mike McCurry avoided commenting on the substance of the charges by Jones, who is seeking $700,000 in damages, and referred reporters to the government's briefs on the narrow constitutional issue to be argued on Monday.

"We've had significant comment on the issue that's before the court today. The issue before the court today is about the presidency and about the constitution and you can read it in our briefs," McCurry told reporters.

In written arguments submitted to the high court, Clinton's attorney, Robert Bennett, said civil lawsuits against a sitting president must be delayed because they would be "burdensome and disruptive," distracting him from the duties of the job. He said no U.S. president had ever been required to give evidence in a civil proceeding, much less appear as a defendant in court.

The White House has been determined to focus attention on the constitutional issue at stake rather than on the suit's allegations, already publicly detailed by Jones, which revive memories of Clinton's one-time reputation as a philanderer.

Clinton himself will be spending his day in a presidential manner, awarding Medals of Honour, the military's highest award, at 11:00 a.m. (1600 GMT) and then working on his inaugural address, which he is to deliver on Jan. 20.

Asked on Friday if the hearing would be a distraction, Clinton said, "I don't have any control over what anyone else does; I can only control what I do. It's not going to cause me any difficulty because I'm going to do my job here."
McCurry said he did not know how Clinton would be briefed on the presentation of Monday's arguments but said White House Counsel Jack Quinn would attend the Supreme Court session.

There have been efforts to settle the case out of court, once before it was filed and again in June before the Supreme Court decided to hear Clinton's appeal that the lawsuit should be delayed, lawyers familiar with the talks have said.
